passage: In the village school, the slate pencils always broke by noon. Preeti had two new ones in her tin. Vijay, on the next mat, had broken his and was chewing the stub. "Can I use one?" he whispered. Preeti looked at his rubber, a smooth green one shaped like a mango. "Only if I can use your rubber for the whole day." Vijay hesitated. "Half the day?" "Whole day. That's fair. One pencil, one rubber." He handed it over. Preeti gave him the pencil and felt satisfied. That was the right way; nobody lost. When the teacher asked why she had two rubbers on her mat, Preeti explained the deal proudly.

qa.q: What shape was Vijay's rubber?
qa.a: Shaped like a mango.

qa.q: Why did Preeti feel satisfied after the swap?
qa.a: She felt it was fair because each of them gave one thing and got one thing back, so nobody lost.

qa.q: What could the teacher ask Preeti to help her think beyond the deal?
qa.a: The teacher could ask how Vijay felt chewing a broken stub, helping Preeti see his need, not just the trade.

qa.q: How might Vijay see the deal?
qa.a: Vijay may feel a little cheated, having to give his rubber for the whole day just to write, but he agreed because he needed the pencil.

grounding: A child will share her pencil only in exchange for a rubber, judging fairness as an even trade for herself.

passage: At lunch in the school cafeteria in Vancouver, Javier eyed Chen's dumplings. "Can I have one?" Chen was eyeing Javier's chocolate chip cookie. "Only if I get half your cookie." "Half? For one dumpling?" "It's a big dumpling." Javier thought about it very seriously. "Okay. One dumpling, half cookie. Deal." They shook hands across the table like businessmen. Later, a new boy sat alone with no lunch at all. Javier noticed him. He looked at his remaining half cookie. Then he looked at the new boy. "He doesn't have anything to trade," he told Chen, and kept the cookie in his box.

qa.q: What did Chen want in exchange for a dumpling?
qa.a: Half of Javier's cookie.

qa.q: Why did Javier keep the cookie when he saw the new boy?
qa.a: He thought sharing only made sense as a trade, and the new boy had nothing to give back, so to Javier it wasn't a fair deal.

qa.q: What could Javier try if he wanted to be kind next time?
qa.a: He could offer part of his cookie to the new boy without asking for anything, just because the boy has no lunch.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel sitting alone with no lunch?
qa.a: He probably feels lonely and hungry, watching others trade food while nobody offers him anything 😔

grounding: Two children trade food as a fair deal, and one keeps his cookie from a boy who has nothing to trade.

passage: At the summer camp, there was only one good swing, the one under the neem tree. Jahnavi got there first and kicked her legs high. Rafiq came up. "Can I have a turn?" Jahnavi kept swinging. "You push me twenty times. Then I'll push you twenty times. That's fair." Rafiq pushed, counting out loud. At nineteen, the camp leader blew the whistle for lunch. "You still owe me twenty," Rafiq said. "No, you owe me one," Jahnavi said. "You only did nineteen." Rafiq's face fell. The camp leader heard. "What would be fair for Rafiq, who hasn't swung at all?" Jahnavi thought. "Twenty-one?" "Maybe after lunch you could push him first." Jahnavi shrugged. "If he pushes me back."

qa.q: Where was the one good swing?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Jahnavi said he owed her one?
qa.a: Rafiq felt let down and unfairly treated, since he had pushed her but never got a turn.

qa.q: What did the camp leader's question try to do?
qa.a: It tried to get Jahnavi to think about Rafiq's side, not just her count, though she still sees it as a trade.

qa.q: If you were Rafiq, what would you want from Jahnavi?
qa.a: Rafiq would probably want a turn without more conditions, since he already did most of the work pushing her.

grounding: At camp a child insists on an even swap of swing pushes, judging fairness by what she gets back.

passage:
I'm Devika. I sit next to Wasim in Class 4, and he's funny, but he runs everything like a shop.
In art on Tuesday, I forgot my sharpener. I asked to borrow his. He said, "Okay, but I'll use your blue crayon for the whole class." I said fine.
Then the new boy, Ronit, asked Wasim for his eraser because he'd rubbed a hole in his page. Wasim looked at Ronit's pencil box, which was almost empty. "What will you give me?" Ronit had nothing. So Wasim said, "Then no." He didn't say it meanly. He said it like a rule.
After class I asked him why. He shrugged. "If I give free, then everyone takes free. I'll share my pencil if you share your eraser. That's fair."
I don't know if he even noticed Ronit's face. Ronit had to fix his page with his finger.

qa.q: What did Wasim want in exchange for his sharpener?
qa.a: To use Devika's blue crayon for the whole class.

qa.q: What does Wasim's saying 'If I give free, then everyone takes free' show about how he thinks?
qa.a: It shows he judges what's right by whether he gets a fair return, so Ronit's need didn't count once Ronit had nothing to trade.

qa.q: At which moment could Wasim have made a different choice?
qa.a: When Ronit had nothing to give, Wasim could have lent the eraser anyway, seeing Ronit's torn page instead of only the missing trade.

qa.q: How might Ronit have felt when Wasim refused him?
qa.a: Ronit, as the new boy with an almost empty pencil box, probably felt embarrassed and left out, having to fix his page with his finger.

grounding: It shows, through a classmate's eyes, a child who shares only in fair exchanges, so another child's need matters to him only as part of a trade.

passage:
Monday. Afreen had forgotten her ruler. Zubin, eight, held his up. "You can use it if I get your eraser for the whole day." Afreen agreed. Zubin looked pleased. A fair deal.
Wednesday. Zubin's water bottle leaked all over his bag in the hot sun at PE. Afreen held out hers without a word. Zubin drank, then said seriously, "Okay. Now I owe you one water." He wrote it on his hand in pen: A: 1 water.
Friday. On sports day, Afreen's shoelace came undone right before her race. Zubin knelt and tied it fast. Then he rubbed the ink off his hand. "There. Now we're even."
Afreen laughed and ran. Zubin watched, glad the count was back to zero.

qa.q: What did Zubin write on his hand?
qa.a: A: 1 water.

qa.q: Why did Zubin feel glad when the count was back to zero?
qa.a: He sees helping as a fair trade, so owing Afreen made him uneasy and being even felt right to him.

qa.q: What could a teacher or friend help Zubin notice about Afreen's water on Wednesday?
qa.a: They could point out that Afreen shared without asking for anything, helping him see kindness can be given freely, not only traded.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Zubin's 'Now we're even'?
qa.a: Afreen seems amused rather than hurt, perhaps finding his careful counting funny, since she helped him without keeping score.

grounding: It shows over several days a child who judges fairness by even exchanges, keeping count of favours so that others' needs matter mainly as part of the trade.

passage:
Class 3 note, Tuesday, art period.
Gopika, eight, wanted Shreya's glitter pen. She didn't ask to borrow it. She made an offer: "I'll give you two of my stickers if you let me use the glitter pen for the whole period."
Shreya thought about it and said, "Three stickers."
"Two and a half," Gopika said, very seriously. They settled on three.
Later, when a new girl had no crayons, Gopika held hers back. "What will she give me?" she asked me.
I didn't scold her. At her age, fair often means a good exchange for yourself.
What I did next: I said the new girl had nothing to trade today, and asked Gopika what she thought we could do. She thought, then lent two crayons "until tomorrow".

qa.q: How many stickers did Gopika and Shreya settle on?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Gopika thinking when she asked what the new girl would give her?
qa.a: She felt that sharing should be a fair trade, and was unsure why she should give without getting something back.

qa.q: How did the note-writer respond, and why is it wise?
qa.a: They didn't scold but asked Gopika what could be done, which let her fair-play instinct stretch towards the new girl's need.

qa.q: How might the new girl have felt when Gopika lent the crayons?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and welcomed after having none.

grounding: It shows a child treating sharing as a fair trade, as noted by a teacher who gently widens it.

passage:
Friday
Today I made the best deal. Madhav needed an eraser in the maths test. I said I'll give you mine if you give me your pencil sharpener for the whole week. He said okay.
That's fair. He gets something, I get something.
But then Kiran asked for my ruler and he had nothing to give me. So I said no. Kiran looked sad. Madhav said I was being mean.
I don't think I'm mean. If I just give everyone everything, what do I get? Nothing. That's not fair.
Mumma said at dinner, "What if you're the one without a ruler one day?" I said then I'll trade something.
But what if I have nothing to trade? I didn't think about that.
– Yash

qa.q: What did Yash get from Madhav for the eraser?
qa.a: Madhav's pencil sharpener for the whole week.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Madhav called it mean?
qa.a: Yash felt defensive and unsure, believing fair meant a trade but starting to wonder.

qa.q: What could help Yash think beyond the deal?
qa.a: A parent or teacher could keep asking questions like Mumma's about having nothing to trade, helping Yash notice others' needs.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt when Yash said no?
qa.a: Kiran probably felt sad and left out, having nothing to trade for the ruler.

grounding: It shows a child judging fairness by what gives a good exchange for himself, with others' needs part of the trade.

passage:
Under the mango tree behind the village school, Jagdish, eight, sat with his tin of marbles. Ganga, his friend, had a bag of raw mangoes from her grandfather's tree.
"Three marbles for two mangoes," Jagdish said.
"Four marbles."
"Three and the blue one."
"Deal."
They both grinned. It was fair.
Then little Pappu came, his hands empty, staring at the mangoes.
"What will you give?" Jagdish asked him.
"Nothing. I don't have anything."
"Then no mango." Jagdish said it simply, like a rule.
Ganga hesitated, then gave Pappu a small one anyway. Jagdish frowned. "That's not fair. He didn't give you anything."
Ganga shrugged. "He's small."

qa.q: What was Jagdish trading for the mangoes?
qa.a: Three marbles and the blue one.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when Ganga gave Pappu a mango?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and a bit annoyed, because to him fairness meant an exchange.

qa.q: How could a teacher help Jagdish see beyond the trade?
qa.a: A teacher could ask him how Pappu might feel with no mango, gently pointing to feelings without shaming his sense of fair play.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Pappu's empty hands?
qa.a: Ganga sees that Pappu is small and has nothing, and gives out of kindness rather than trade.

grounding: It shows a child judging fairness as a deal, where others' needs matter mainly as part of the trade.

passage:
In the classroom in Oslo, Ingrid, nine, had the only blue marker in the group. Nkechi asked, "Can I borrow it for the sky?"
Ingrid held it tight. "What will you give me?"
"Um... what do you want?"
"Your sparkly eraser for the rest of the lesson."
"That's not the same!"
"It is. You get something, I get something. That's fair."
Nkechi sighed and handed over the eraser. Ingrid gave her the marker.
Later Nkechi's pencil broke and she had no sharpener. Ingrid had one. She didn't offer, until Nkechi said, "I'll give the eraser back if you lend it." Ingrid nodded. "Deal."

qa.q: What did Ingrid want in exchange for the blue marker?
qa.a: Nkechi's sparkly eraser for the rest of the lesson.

qa.q: Why did Ingrid ask what Nkechi would give her?
qa.a: She felt protective of the only blue marker and believed fairness meant a trade, so she wanted something for herself in return.

qa.q: How could a teacher help Ingrid see sharing beyond trades?
qa.a: Ask how Nkechi feels without the marker, and point out times someone helped Ingrid without asking for anything back.

qa.q: How does Nkechi see Ingrid's trades?
qa.a: Nkechi feels they are unequal and a bit frustrating, but goes along to get what she needs.

grounding: A child treats sharing as a fair trade, lending a marker only for an eraser, and others' needs matter mainly as part of the deal.

passage:
In the school library in Ranchi, Damini's compass had gone missing just before the geometry test. Tanvir, beside her, had two.
"Tanvir, please lend me one?"
Tanvir, eleven, thought. "Okay. But you have to let me copy your English homework later."
"That's cheating."
"Then give me your chocolate from lunch."
"Fine."
The librarian overheard and said, "Tanvir, would you lend it without a deal?"
Tanvir frowned, genuinely puzzled. "But then I get nothing. That's not fair to me."
Damini took the compass and the chocolate deal. Tanvir looked satisfied. To him, the world was balanced.

qa.q: What did Tanvir first ask for in exchange?
qa.a: He asked to copy Damini's English homework later.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir genuinely puzzled by the librarian's question?
qa.a: He believed lending without a deal meant he got nothing, which felt unfair to him; fairness to him meant an equal trade.

qa.q: What could the librarian say next to help Tanvir look beyond the deal?
qa.a: Ask how Damini would feel without a compass in the test, or whether Tanvir would like help from someone if his went missing.

qa.q: How might Damini feel about having to trade her chocolate?
qa.a: She might feel a bit annoyed or disappointed, but relieved to have the compass for the test.

grounding: A child lends a compass only in exchange for chocolate, judging fairness by what he gets back.

passage:
Monday: At recess, Naveen offered Vasudha a share of his mango slices. Vasudha said, "What do I have to give you?" Naveen shrugged. "Nothing." Vasudha, ten, looked suspicious, then gave him a biscuit anyway. "Now it's fair."

passage: Aparna, you're counting who gave you what on your birthday, so let me tell you about me at eight. It was Lohri, and Balwinder had the best kite in the village, red with a long tail. I had two sugarcane sticks and nothing else. 'I'll give you one stick if you give me the kite for ten minutes,' I said. Fair, na? He agreed. passage: Fog had made the school bus forty minutes late, and the half-yearly maths test was starting in five minutes. Nirmala slid into the seat next to Samir, breathless, and pressed her pencil to the paper. The tip snapped. 'Samir, sharpener? Please, quick!' Samir had a sharpener, a new blue one. qa.q: What could Samir do next time a classmate is in a rush like this?

passage: It was Navroz week, and the Parsi colony hall in Mumbai smelled of falooda and fresh paint. The children were making greeting cards at long tables.
